messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Alessandro's world was forever altered on a crisp autumn evening two years ago, when his younger brother, Luca, was brutally attacked by a group of strangers while walking home from a friend's house. Alessandro, then 19, had been waiting up for Luca, and it was he who received the frantic call from their mother, informing him that Luca had been rushed to the hospital with severe injuries. The memory of that night is etched in Alessandro's mind like a series of photographs - the sound of his mother's panicked voice, the feeling of helplessness as he sped to the hospital, and the sight of Luca's battered body lying motionless on the ICU bed. In the months that followed, Alessandro became increasingly consumed by the need to protect himself and those around him from potential harm. He began to notice suspicious behavior in others - a stranger glancing at his family too long, a friend joking about violence - and would immediately go on high alert, his body tensing up as if ready to spring into action. Comments about family or loved ones being hurt would send him spiraling into dark thoughts of what could have been, and the sight of specific body parts - broken bones, cuts, or bruises - would transport him back to that terrible night. Alessandro tried to cope with these feelings by avoiding media coverage of similar events, switching off the TV whenever a violent crime story came on, and steering clear of online articles about attacks on innocent people. He couldn't bear the thought of being alone in a room or building, as if the absence of others would leave him vulnerable to some unseen threat. But despite these efforts, he found himself increasingly isolated - unable to work due to anxiety, his relationships with friends and family strained by his constant vigilance. As time went on, Alessandro began to turn his frustration inward, physically harming himself in an attempt to release the overwhelming feelings of guilt, anger, and fear that had taken up residence inside him. His sleep grew fitful, punctuated by sudden movements or noises that would jolt him awake, leaving him breathless and disoriented. He started experiencing flashbacks - vivid, visceral replays of that autumn night, complete with the scent of antiseptic and blood that seemed to cling to his nostrils even years later. Alessandro struggled to verbalize his memories of the event, as if the words themselves might unleash a fresh wave of pain. When he did try to talk about it, the images came flooding back - Luca's swollen face, the beeping machines in the ICU, the numb feeling that had settled over him like a shroud. Alessandro felt like his body was working against him, perpetually on high alert even when logic told him he was safe. He'd lost faith in himself, unable to shake the conviction that he was no longer capable of protecting those he loved or doing the things that once defined him. His mind had become a constant battlefield, with fears and doubts vying for dominance. Lately, Alessandro's marriage has begun to suffer under the weight of his anxiety and withdrawal. His wife, tired of walking on eggshells around him, has started to feel like she's losing her partner to this sea of PTSD symptoms. It was her gentle insistence that he seek help that finally brought Alessandro to therapy - a step he hopes will lead him out of this darkness and back into the world of the living. For now, though, he remains trapped in this never-ending cycle of fear, his mind whispering an insistent refrain: you're not safe, you'll never be safe again.
